documentNotes.title: 2006 Semi-Final Exam — Instructions
documentNotes.statement:
AAPT / AIP — United States Physics Team 2006.

DO NOT OPEN THIS TEST UNTIL YOU ARE TOLD TO BEGIN

- Work Part A first. You have 90 minutes to complete all four problems.
- After you have completed Part A, you may take a break.
- Then work Part B. You have 90 minutes to complete both problems.
- Show all your work. Partial credit will be given.
- Start each question on a new sheet of paper. Be sure to put your name in the upper right-hand corner of each page, along with the question number and the page number/total pages for this problem. For example: Doe, Jamie; A1 – 1/3.
- A hand-held calculator may be used. Its memory must be cleared of data and programs. You may use only the basic functions found on a simple scientific calculator. Calculators may not be shared. Cell phones, PDA’s, or cameras may not be used during the exam or while the exam papers are present. You may not use any tables, books, or collections of formulas.
- Questions with the same point value are not necessarily of the same difficulty.
- Do not discuss the contents of this exam with anyone until after March 20th.
- Good luck!

problems.statement:
An otherwise uniform disk of radius $R$ has a circular hole of radius $R/2$ cut out so that the hole touches both the center and the edge of the disk. The disk has a mass $M$ after the hole is cut out. The disk is placed above a wheel so that when the lower wheel rotates, the disk will rotate with a constant angular velocity. The disk is constrained so that it can only move in the up and down direction or rotate freely. If the angular velocity of the disk exceeds a certain value, $\omega_{\max}$, the disk will bounce up and down on the lower wheel. Find the total kinetic energy of the disk when the angular velocity is $\omega_{\max}$. Express your answer in terms of $M$, $R$, and $g$ (but not in terms of $\omega_{\max}$).

[[figure:p1-fig1]]

figures.alt: Disk with an off-center circular hole resting on a lower wheel.

solution.statement:
Source note: the key says “to the right” for the center of mass, while its algebra uses $-r$ and the question figure places the hole on the right. The printed wording is retained.

Sooner or later we need to find both the location of the center of mass $r$ and the rotational inertia $I$ about the axis of rotation. Let’s do these two things first.

We can treat the top disk as a solid disk of mass $M_s$ with a hole of mass $M_h$ cut out. Since the radius of the hole is half the radius of the disk, we can conclude that

$$M_h=\frac{\pi(R/2)^2}{\pi R^2}M_s=\frac14M_s,\tag{A1-1}$$

so

$$M=M_s-M_h=\frac34M_s=3M_h.\tag{A1-2}$$

By symmetry the center of mass will be on a line connecting the centers of both the hole and the disk, and must be located a distance $r$ to the right of the center of the disk, where

$$M_s(0)=M(-r)+M_h\frac R2.\tag{A1-3}$$

Then

$$r=\frac R6.\tag{A1-4}$$

We can apply a similar approach to find the rotational inertia about the axis of rotation:

$$I_s=I+I_h,\tag{A1-5}$$

where $I_s$ is the rotational inertia of a solid disk and $I_h$ is the rotational inertia of the part that used to be in the hole, both measured about the axis of rotation. $I_s$ is easy,

$$I_s=\frac12M_sR^2=\frac23MR^2,\tag{A1-6}$$

while $I_h$ requires an application of the parallel axis theorem,

$$I_h=\frac12M_h\left(\frac R2\right)^2+M_h\left(\frac R2\right)^2=\frac18MR^2.\tag{A1-7}$$

Finally,

$$I=I_s-I_h=\frac{13}{24}MR^2.\tag{A1-8}$$

Now consider the motion of the center of mass. It is rotating about the axis of rotation with an angular speed $\omega$, so that the magnitude of the acceleration of the center of mass is given by

$$a=r\omega^2.\tag{A1-9}$$

The net force on the disk when the center of mass is at the top is then given by

$$F_{\rm net}=Mg-F_N=Mr\omega^2,\tag{A1-10}$$

where $F_N$ is the normal force. The disk begins to hop when the normal force is zero, so

$$\omega^2=\frac gr=\frac{6g}{R}.\tag{A1-11}$$

The total kinetic energy is then

$$K=\frac12I\omega^2=\frac12\left(\frac{13}{24}MR^2\right)\left(\frac{6g}{R}\right)=\frac{13}{8}MgR.\tag{A1-12}$$

problems.statement:
A parallel plate capacitor is constructed from two vertical square conducting surfaces with sides of length $L$ separated horizontally by a distance $2d$. Assume that $d\ll L$, so that fringing effects can be neglected. The plates are charged to $Q$ and $-Q$, and then electrically isolated. A square conducting slab, also with sides of length $L$, but with thickness $d$, is then inserted vertically between the two plates without making contact with either plate. Assume that the slab moves only in the vertical direction. Give your answers to each part only in terms of the variables listed above and any appropriate fundamental constants.

[[figure:p2-fig1]]

figures.alt: Capacitor with plate separation2d and heightL, inserted slab thicknessd and insertiony, downward gravityg.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find an expression for the capacitance $C$ of the system assuming that the movable slab extends inward between the plates by a distance $y$.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Find an expression for the mass of the slab $m$ given that the equilibrium location (where the force of gravity on the slab is balanced by the attraction into the capacitor) for the slab is $y=L/2$.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: The slab is perturbed vertically slightly from its equilibrium position so that it undergoes simple harmonic motion. Find an expression for the frequency of the motion of the slab.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
Treat the system as two capacitors in parallel. One has a spacing of $2d$ and a surface area of $L(L-y)$, the other a spacing of $2d-d$ and a surface area of $Ly$. The capacitance is then found from the formula $\epsilon_0A/d$ and the rule for capacitors in parallel to be

$$C=\frac{\epsilon_0L(L-y)}{2d}+\frac{\epsilon_0Ly}{d}=\frac{\epsilon_0L(L+y)}{2d}.\tag{A2-1}$$

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
The potential energy stored in the capacitor is given by

$$U=\frac12\frac{Q^2}{C},\tag{A2-2}$$

so the electric force of attraction on the slab is

$$F=-\frac{\partial U}{\partial y}\tag{A2-3}$$

$$=\frac{Q^2}{2C^2}\frac{\partial C}{\partial y}\tag{A2-4}$$

$$=\frac{dQ^2}{\epsilon_0L(L+y)^2}.\tag{A2-5}$$

But this is equal to the force from gravity, $mg$, when $y=L/2$, so

$$m=\frac{dQ^2}{\epsilon_0gL(L+L/2)^2}=\frac{4dQ^2}{9\epsilon_0gL^3}.\tag{A2-6}$$

sections.title: c.
sections.statement:
We need to expand the expression for the force about the point $y=L/2$. Letting $y=L/2+x$, we get

$$F=\frac{dQ^2}{\epsilon_0L(3L/2+x)^2}\tag{A2-7}$$

$$=\frac{4dQ^2}{9\epsilon_0L^3}\left(1+\frac{2x}{3L}\right)^{-2}\tag{A2-8}$$

$$\approx\frac{4dQ^2}{9\epsilon_0L^3}\left(1-2\frac{2x}{3L}\right)\tag{A2-9}$$

$$=\frac{4dQ^2}{9\epsilon_0L^3}-\frac{16dQ^2}{27\epsilon_0L^4}x.\tag{A2-10}$$

We know the first term in the last line balances gravity; it is the second term that is of interest. It is useful to write it in terms of the mass,

$$\Delta F=-\frac{16dQ^2}{27\epsilon_0L^4}x=-\frac{4mg}{3L}x,\tag{A2-11}$$

so that the effective spring constant $k$ is given by

$$k=\frac{4mg}{3L}.\tag{A2-12}$$

The frequency of small oscillations is then

$$f=\frac1{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac km}=\frac1\pi\sqrt{\frac g{3L}}.\tag{A2-13}$$

problems.statement:
A hollow vertical cylinder contains a solid cylindrical piston with length $h$. The cylindrical piston is originally held in place by a retaining pin so that a fixed amount of gas at temperature $T_0$ and pressure $p_0$ is trapped beneath the piston. $T_0$ and $p_0$ are also the temperature and pressure of the gas outside the cylinder. The bottom of the piston is originally a height $y_0$ above the bottom of the cylinder.

When the retaining pin is removed, the piston falls under the influence of gravity, compressing the gas so that the piston drops to $y_1=y_0/8$ before bouncing back up. This process occurs so quickly that no heat enters or leaves the gas.

[[figure:p3-fig1]]

The piston bounces up and down, but eventually comes to rest at a height $y_2$ when the gas in the cylinder is once again in thermal equilibrium with the surroundings. The specific heat capacity at constant volume of the gas in the cylinder is $C_V=\frac32R$.

figures.alt: Vertical cylinder and piston, with piston lengthh and initial gas heighty0.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Find the density of the piston in terms of $p_0$, $g$, and $h$.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Find the numerical value of the ratio $y_2/y_0$.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
First find $\gamma$:

$$\gamma=\frac{C_P}{C_V}=\frac{C_V+R}{C_V}=\frac{\frac32+1}{\frac32}=\frac53.\tag{A3-1}$$

Fast processes are adiabatic processes, especially when we are told that no heat exchange occurs! This means that $pV^\gamma$ is a constant, and then

$$p_0V_0^\gamma=p_1V_1^\gamma.\tag{A3-2}$$

But

$$pV=nRT,\tag{A3-3}$$

so

$$pV^\gamma=\frac{nRT}{V}V^\gamma=nRTV^{\gamma-1}\tag{A3-4}$$

is a constant. Finally, we can write

$$T_0V_0^{\gamma-1}=T_1V_1^{\gamma-1}.\tag{A3-5}$$

Work is done on the gas by the falling cylinder and the external atmosphere. Hence,

$$W=mg(y_0-y_1)+p_0(V_0-V_1),\tag{A3-6}$$

where $m$ is the mass of the piston. But the cross sections, $A$, are uniform, so we can write $V=Ay$ and then the work done is

$$W=(mg+p_0A)(y_0-y_1).\tag{A3-7}$$

This work must equal the change in internal energy of the gas,

$$W=\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T=nC_VT_0\left(\frac{T_1}{T_0}-1\right).\tag{A3-8}$$

But

$$\frac{T_1}{T_0}=\left(\frac{V_0}{V_1}\right)^{\gamma-1},\tag{A3-9}$$

and

$$nC_VT_0=\frac32nRT_0=\frac32p_0V_0,\tag{A3-10}$$

so

$$(mg+p_0A)(y_0-y_1)=\frac32p_0Ay_0\left(\left(\frac{y_0}{y_1}\right)^{\gamma-1}-1\right),\tag{A3-11}$$

or

$$(mg+p_0A)\left(1-\frac{y_1}{y_0}\right)=\frac32p_0A\left(\left(\frac{y_0}{y_1}\right)^{\gamma-1}-1\right).\tag{A3-12}$$

But $y_0=8y_1$, so

$$(mg+p_0A)\left(\frac78\right)=\frac32p_0A(3).\tag{A3-13}$$

Solve for $m$, and

$$m=\frac{29}{7}\frac{p_0A}{g}.\tag{A3-14}$$

We actually want the density, so

$$\rho=\frac{m}{Ah}=\frac{29}{7}\frac{p_0}{gh}.\tag{A3-15}$$

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
Eventually the gas temperature returns to $T_0$ and then

$$p_0V_0=p_2V_2.\tag{A3-16}$$

The pressure will rise to the point that it can support the cylinder,

$$mg=A(p_2-p_0),\tag{A3-17}$$

so

$$mg=Ap_0\left(\frac{V_0}{V_2}-1\right).\tag{A3-18}$$

Rewriting in terms of the ratio $y_0/y_2$,

$$\frac{y_0}{y_2}=\frac{mg}{p_0A}+1\tag{A3-19}$$

$$=\frac{29}{7}+1,\tag{A3-20}$$

$$=\frac{36}{7},\tag{A3-21}$$

and then

$$\frac{y_2}{y_0}=\frac7{36}.\tag{A3-22}$$

problems.statement:
A cyclotron is a particle accelerator consisting of dipole magnets that create two semi-circular regions of magnetic field $B$, pointing uniformly down (toward the bottom of the page). These regions are called “Dees” due to their D shape. The two Dees are placed back-to-back, but with a small separation. Consider a small cyclotron of radius $R$. An AC potential $V=V_0\sin\omega t$, that is switched on at $t=0$, is applied across the Dee electrodes. The particles are accelerated whenever they cross the gap between the electrodes. The gap is small enough that any variation in $V(t)$ during the time it takes a particle to cross the gap may be neglected.

[[figure:p4-fig1]]

(Source: Wikne, Jon. Oslo Cyclotron Laboratory. 1994. 14 Feb. 2006. [http://lynx.uio.no/cycdescr.html](http://lynx.uio.no/cycdescr.html).)

The cyclotron is filled with a variety of ions of different masses, but each has the same charge $q$. All ions start at the center of the cyclotron and are emitted when they reach the edge of the cyclotron. An ion will make many laps around the cyclotron before being emitted. Ignore relativistic effects in parts (a)–(c).

In terms of $\omega$, $q$, $V_0$, $R$, and $B$,

figures.alt: Cyclotron with two electromagnets, Dee electrodes, alternating voltage source and downward fieldB.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: What is the maximum possible momentum of an emitted ion?

parts.label: b.
parts.statement: Of all of the possible ions that satisfy part (a), what is the kinetic energy of the ion emitted first?

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: At what time $t$ after turning on the AC potential are the ions from part (b) emitted?

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: Such a device won’t work well with electrons, as relativistic effects can’t be ignored for energies above one hundred thousand electron-volts. One possible correction is to create a magnetic field that is not constant, but varies with distance from the center of the cyclotron. This enhanced device is called an isochronous cyclotron. Find an expression for the necessary magnetic field $B$ in terms of $r$, $\omega$, $m$ (the mass of the electron), and $q$ (the charge on the electron). Relativistic effects must be considered.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
The ions move, for the most part, in uniform circular motion under the influence of a magnetic force, so

$$\frac{mv^2}{r}=qvB,\tag{A4-1}$$

or

$$mv=qBr.\tag{A4-2}$$

When $r=R$ we have the maximum possible momentum, so

$$p_{\max}=qBR.\tag{A4-3}$$

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
Since

$$K=\frac{p^2}{2m},\tag{A4-4}$$

we have

$$K=\frac{q^2B^2R^2}{2m}.\tag{A4-5}$$

But

$$m=qB\frac Rv=\frac{qB}{\omega},\tag{A4-6}$$

so

$$K=\frac{qBR^2\omega}{2}.\tag{A4-7}$$

sections.title: c.
sections.statement:
The ions pick up this kinetic energy from the changing potential, collecting $2qV_0$ after every revolution. The number of revolutions required is then

$$N=\frac{BR^2\omega}{4V_0},\tag{A4-8}$$

and since each revolution requires a time $2\pi/\omega$, the total time $t$ is given by

$$t=\frac{\pi BR^2}{2V_0}.\tag{A4-9}$$

sections.title: d.
sections.statement:
The cyclotron works only because the revolution of the charged particle is constant in time. $p=qBr$ is relativistically correct, but now the velocity is given by the condition that $p=\gamma mv$. The angular frequency of revolution needs to be $\omega$ in order to get a boost each half-cycle, so

$$v=r\omega.\tag{A4-10}$$

Then

$$p=m\frac v{\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}}=\frac{mr\omega}{\sqrt{1-r^2\omega^2/c^2}}.\tag{A4-11}$$

Putting this into the momentum expression yields

$$B=\frac{m\omega}{q}\left(1-\frac{r^2\omega^2}{c^2}\right)^{-1/2}.\tag{A4-12}$$

problems.statement:
Consider a wire loop of width $X$ and height $D$. The loop is held at rest vertically. There is a uniform magnetic field $B$ passing through the loop. However, the magnetic field abruptly decreases to zero everywhere below the location of the bottom edge of the loop at $t=0$. The magnetic field is perpendicular to the plane of the loop. The mass of the loop is $m$. At time $t=0$, the loop is released from rest so that it begins to fall out of the magnetic field. Let $y(t)$ be the distance that the bottom edge has traveled out of the magnetic field at $t$ seconds after the loop has been released. $y(0)=0$.

[[figure:p5-fig1]]

figures.alt: Rectangular wire loop widthX heightD falling downwards out of the dotted uniform magnetic field; displacementy(t).

sections.title: a.
sections.statement: For simplicity we write $v_t$ instead of $v_{\rm term}$. Wherever possible we will solve the problem in the simplest possible manner.

parts.label: i.
parts.statement:
The magnitude of the force of gravity on the wire is

$$F_g=mg,\tag{B1-1}$$

the magnitude of the magnetic force on a current $I$ in the wire is

$$F_m=BIX,\tag{B1-2}$$

the induced emf, $V$, in the wire when traveling with speed $v$ is

$$V=-BvX,\tag{B1-3}$$

and finally, the relationship between the emf and current is

$$V=IR.\tag{B1-4}$$

Terminal velocity occurs when there is no acceleration, so that the net force is zero. Then

$$mg=BIX,\tag{B1-5}$$

$$mg=B\frac VRX,\tag{B1-6}$$

$$mg=-B\frac{BvX}{R}X,\tag{B1-7}$$

$$-\frac{mgR}{B^2X^2}=v.\tag{B1-8}$$

It is traditional to give the terminal speed, and consequently we don’t usually write the negative sign indicating downward motion. Henceforth,

$$v_t=\frac{mgR}{B^2X^2}.\tag{B1-9}$$

parts.label: ii.
parts.statement:
Let the above symbols, except for $v_t$, now be variables in time. Define a dot notation for time derivatives, so that velocity is given by

$$v=\frac{dy}{dt}=\dot y,\tag{B1-10}$$

and

$$a=\frac{dv}{dt}=\dot v=\ddot y.\tag{B1-11}$$

The acceleration of the wire is given by Newton’s second law,

$$ma=F_m-F_g,\tag{B1-12}$$

$$m\dot v=BIX-mg,\tag{B1-13}$$

$$m\dot v=-B\frac{BvX}{R}X-mg,\tag{B1-14}$$

$$\dot v=-\frac{B^2X^2}{mR}v-mg,\tag{B1-15}$$

$$\dot v=-g\left(\frac v{v_t}+1\right).\tag{B1-16}$$

$$\tag{B1-17}$$

We must now integrate this expression,

$$\frac{dv}{dt}=-g\left(\frac v{v_t}+1\right),\tag{B1-18}$$

$$\frac{dv}{(v+v_t)}=-\frac g{v_t}\,dt,\tag{B1-19}$$

$$\int\frac{dv}{(v+v_t)}=-\int\frac g{v_t}\,dt,\tag{B1-20}$$

$$\ln\left(\frac v{v_t}+1\right)=-\frac{gt}{v_t}.\tag{B1-21}$$

Solving for $v$:

$$v=v_t\left(e^{-gt/v_t}-1\right).\tag{B1-22}$$

parts.label: iii.
parts.statement:
Thermal energy dissipates at a rate given by

$$P=IV=V^2/R,\tag{B1-23}$$

so

$$P=\frac{B^2v^2X^2}{R}\tag{B1-24}$$

$$=mgv_t\left(e^{-gt/v_t}-1\right)^2.\tag{B1-25}$$

parts.label: iv.
parts.statement:
It is tempting to integrate the above expression. Don’t do it! Instead, focus on the fact that the energy dissipated is equal to the change in energy of the wire. Note that it is moving at terminal speed when it completely leaves the field region, so

$$E=mgD-\frac12mv_t^2.\tag{B1-26}$$

sections.title: b.
sections.statement: Be warned that we never actually need to find $L$ in this problem, so don’t spend time trying to calculate it!

parts.label: i.
parts.statement:
Equations B1-1, B1-2, and B1-3 are still true. But now the emf is related to the inductance and the change in current by

$$V=-L\dot I.\tag{B1-27}$$

The dot above the $I$ means time derivative. Combining,

$$m\dot v=BIX-mg,\tag{B1-28}$$

$$m\ddot v=B\dot I X,\tag{B1-29}$$

$$=-B\frac VLX,\tag{B1-30}$$

$$=-\frac{B^2X^2}{L}v.\tag{B1-31}$$

This is the differential equation for a simple harmonic oscillator, with angular frequency $\omega$ given by

$$\omega=\sqrt{\frac{B^2X^2}{mL}}.\tag{B1-32}$$

The period of oscillation is then

$$T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}=\frac{2\pi\sqrt{mL}}{BX}.\tag{B1-33}$$

parts.label: ii.
parts.statement:
Oscillatory motion is necessarily of the form

$$y=A\cos(\omega t+\phi)+B,\tag{B1-34}$$

where $A$, $B$, and $\phi$ are constants. Since $y$ is a maximum when $t=0$, we can conclude that $\phi=0$. The acceleration will be given by $a=\ddot y$, and the maximum acceleration is then $a_{\max}=A\omega^2$. This maximum acceleration occurs when the object is released, and there is not yet any current through the wire, so, from Eq. B1-28,

$$mA\omega^2=mg,\tag{B1-35}$$

$$A=\frac{mgL}{B^2X^2}.\tag{B1-36}$$

Finally, $y=D$ when $t=0$, so

$$y=A\cos\omega t+D-A,\tag{B1-37}$$

$$=\frac{mgL}{B^2X^2}\left(\cos\left(\sqrt{\frac{B^2X^2}{mL}}\,t\right)-1\right)+D.\tag{B1-38}$$

parts.label: iii.
parts.statement:
Using $v_{\max}=A\omega$,

$$K_{\max}=\frac12mv_{\max}^2,\tag{B1-39}$$

$$=\frac12m\left(\frac g\omega\right)^2,\tag{B1-40}$$

$$=\frac12\frac{g^2m^2L}{B^2X^2}.\tag{B1-41}$$

parts.label: iv.
parts.statement:
At the bottom point of the path all of the “lost” potential energy of the wire must be stored in the magnetic field, so

$$E_B=2mgA=\frac{2m^2g^2L}{B^2X^2}.\tag{B1-42}$$

parts.label: v.
parts.statement:
At the low point of the oscillation the magnetic energy will be maximal, or

$$t_{\max}=\frac T2=\frac{\pi\sqrt{mL}}{BX}.\tag{B1-43}$$

sections.title: a.
sections.statement: Suppose that the loop has resistance $R$ but negligible inductance. Assume that $D$ is large enough that the loop very nearly reaches terminal velocity before the loop entirely falls out of the magnetic field. Express your answers to part (a) in terms of $X$, $D$, $B$, $m$, $g$, $R$, and $t$.

parts.label: i.
parts.statement: Find the terminal velocity, $v_{\rm term}$, of the loop.

parts.label: ii.
parts.statement:
Answers to part (a) ii–iv may include the symbol $v_{\rm term}$ in addition to any of the symbols listed above.

Derive an expression for velocity as a function of time that is valid until the loop is entirely out of the magnetic field.

parts.label: iii.
parts.statement: Derive an expression for the rate at which thermal energy is dissipated due to the resistance of the loop.

parts.label: iv.
parts.statement: Determine the total amount of thermal energy dissipated from $t=0$ until the time that the top edge of the loop just starts to leave the magnetic field.

sections.title: b.
sections.statement: Suppose instead that the loop is made of a superconducting material so that it has negligible resistance. In this case, we cannot neglect the self-inductance of the loop $L$. Assume that $D$ is large enough that the loop never falls entirely out of the magnetic field. Express your answers to part (b) in terms of $X$, $D$, $B$, $m$, $g$, $L$, and $t$.

parts.label: i.
parts.statement: Prove mathematically that the loop oscillates up and down in simple harmonic motion and determine the period of the oscillation.

parts.label: ii.
parts.statement: Derive an expression for $y(t)$.

parts.label: iii.
parts.statement: Determine the maximum kinetic energy of the loop.

parts.label: iv.
parts.statement: Determine the maximum energy stored in the magnetic field of the loop.

parts.label: v.
parts.statement: At what times is the energy stored in the magnetic field at its maximum value?

problems.statementAfterParts: (Based on a problem by W. M. Saslow, Am. J. Phys. 55, 986 (1987).)

problems.statement:
In this problem, we present a simple model of seasonal temperature variation. We ignore temperature and illumination changes between day and night, considering only daily average values. We also ignore all forms of heat transfer other than radiation, including any heat transfer between areas of the surface of the Earth. Finally, we ignore the effects of the atmosphere and clouds.

We therefore consider a patch of ground with heat capacity **per unit area** $c$ and emissivity $\epsilon$, illuminated by light of varying intensity $I$. The patch therefore has a varying temperature $T$.

figures.alt: Figure1: Relative daily sunlight intensity versus time in years for several latitudes.
Figure2: College Park average daily intensity and sinusoidal fit.
Figure3: BWI normal and record high/low temperatures throughout the year, Fahrenheit and Celsius scales.

solution.statement: Source note: the printed signs in (B2-15) and (B2-16) differ from the preceding and following lines; they are retained as printed. The question’s Figure2 caption prints a minus sign in its fitted sinusoid.

figures.alt: Official predicted temperature difference (Centigrade) versus time lag in months, from0 to3months.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement:
The radiation power absorbed by the patch of area $a$ is

$$\epsilon aI,\tag{B2-1}$$

while the power radiated from the patch is

$$\epsilon a\sigma T^4.\tag{B2-2}$$

The imbalance causes a temperature change given by

$$ca\frac{dT}{dt}=\epsilon aI-\epsilon a\sigma T^4,\tag{B2-3}$$

$$\frac c\epsilon\frac{dT}{dt}=I-\sigma T^4.\tag{B2-4}$$

sections.title: b.
sections.statement:
We will need to do an expansion of $T^4$.

$$T^4=T_0^4\left(1+\frac{T_1}{T_0}\sin(\omega t-\phi)\right)^4,\tag{B2-5}$$

$$\approx T_0^4\left(1+4\frac{T_1}{T_0}\sin(\omega t-\phi)\right).\tag{B2-6}$$

Insert this and the given expression for $I$ into Eq. B2-4,

$$\frac c\epsilon(T_1\omega\cos(\omega t-\phi))=\tag{B2-7}$$

$$I_0+I_1\sin(\omega t)-\sigma T_0^4\left(1+4\frac{T_1}{T_0}\sin(\omega t-\phi)\right),\tag{B2-8}$$

or

$$\sigma T_0^4+4\sigma T_0^3T_1\sin(\omega t-\phi)+\frac{c\omega T_1}{\epsilon}\cos(\omega t-\phi)=I_0+I_1\sin(\omega t).\tag{B2-9}$$

Clearly, then,

$$A=\sigma T_0^4,\tag{B2-10}$$

$$B=4\sigma T_0^3T_1,\tag{B2-11}$$

$$C=\frac{c\omega T_1}{\epsilon}.\tag{B2-12}$$

sections.title: c.
sections.statement:
The only way that it can work is if $A=I_0$. Of course, one would expect the average intensity to be related to the average temperature in this way.

Expand the left hand sine and cosine terms according to the angle addition formulae:

$$\sin(\omega t-\phi)=-\cos\omega t\sin\phi+\sin\omega t\cos\phi,\tag{B2-13}$$

$$\cos(\omega t-\phi)=\cos\omega t\cos\phi+\sin\omega t\sin\phi.\tag{B2-14}$$

Substitute into Equation (1) from the question paper.

$$B(-\cos\omega t\sin\phi+\sin\omega t\cos\phi)+C(\cos\omega t\cos\phi-\sin\omega t\sin\phi)=I_1\sin\omega t.\tag{B2-15}$$

This, after collecting terms, yields

$$(-B\sin\phi-C\cos\phi)\cos\omega t+(B\cos\phi+C\sin\phi)\sin\omega t=I_1\sin\omega t.\tag{B2-16}$$

The cosine term must vanish, and this only happens if

$$-B\sin\phi+C\cos\phi=0,\tag{B2-17}$$

leaving the sine term, so

$$B\cos\phi+C\sin\phi=I_1.\tag{B2-18}$$

Combining,

$$B\cos\phi+B\frac{\sin\phi}{\cos\phi}\sin\phi=I_1,\tag{B2-19}$$

$$B=I_1\cos\phi,\tag{B2-20}$$

and then

$$C=B\frac{\sin\phi}{\cos\phi}=I_1\sin\phi.\tag{B2-21}$$

sections.title: d.
sections.statement:
Evaluate $B/A$.

$$\frac BA=\frac{I_1}{I_0}\cos\phi,\tag{B2-22}$$

and

$$\frac BA=\frac{4\sigma T_0^3T_1}{\sigma T_0^4}=4\frac{T_1}{T_0},\tag{B2-23}$$

we have

$$\frac{I_1}{I_0}\cos\phi=4\frac{T_1}{T_0}.\tag{B2-24}$$

Since $I_1/I_0=0.126/0.244=0.516$ we ought be concerned that $T_1/T_0$ might not be a sufficiently small quantity for this approximation!

sections.title: e.
sections.statement:
Since the temperature difference is twice the oscillation amplitude,

$$\Delta T=2T_1,\tag{B2-25}$$

so we are interested in graphing

$$\Delta T=\frac{T_0}{2}\frac{I_1}{I_0}\cos\phi,\tag{B2-26}$$

$$=(73.1\text{ K})\cos\left(t\frac\pi{6\text{ month}}\right).\tag{B2-27}$$

[[figure:p6-fig4]]

sections.title: f.
sections.statement: According to the data on the question paper the peak temperature happens about one month after the solstice. The predicted summer/winter temperature difference would then be about $62\,\mathrm{C}^\circ$, which is about 2.5 times that seen in the average temperature data for BWI.

sections.title: a.
sections.statement: Develop an equation relating $T$, $\frac{dT}{dt}$, $I$, $c$, $\epsilon$, and the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$.

sections.title: b.–f.
sections.statement:
Figure 1 shows the yearly variation in average daily sunlight intensity on Earth for various latitudes. The variation is not sinusoidal, but for temperate latitudes, it may be approximated as a sinusoid. In particular, Figure 2 shows the variation in College Park, Maryland (at $39^\circ$ N latitude), together with a good sinusoidal approximation. Therefore, we assume that the intensity has the form $I=I_0+I_1\sin(\omega t)$. If the annual variation in temperature is small compared to the absolute temperature, we will likewise have $T=T_0+T_1\sin(\omega t-\phi)$, where by hypothesis $T_1\ll T_0$.

[[figure:p6-fig1]]

Figure 1: Average daily sun intensity on Earth ($23.5^\circ$ axis tilt) for various latitudes. The vertical scale is normalized so that the intensity when the sun is overhead is 1.

[[figure:p6-fig2]]

Figure 2: Average daily sun intensity in College Park, with sinusoidal fit. The fit has equation $0.244-0.126\sin(2\pi t)$.

parts.label: b.
parts.statement:
Show that your previous result now implies an equation of the form

$$A+B\sin(\omega t-\phi)+C\cos(\omega t-\phi)=I_0+I_1\sin(\omega t)\tag{1}$$

and provide the expressions for $A$, $B$, and $C$ in terms of $T_0$, $T_1$, $c$, $\epsilon$, $\sigma$, and $\omega$.

parts.label: c.
parts.statement: Using equation (1), find expressions for $A$, $B$, and $C$ in terms of $I_0$, $I_1$, and $\phi$.

parts.label: d.
parts.statement: Combine your results to obtain a simple relationship between the relative amplitude of intensity fluctuations $I_1/I_0$, the relative amplitude of temperature fluctuations $T_1/T_0$, and the phase shift $\phi$.

parts.label: e.
parts.statement: Plot on graph paper the predicted difference between summer and winter temperatures in Kelvin vs. the number of months between the summer solstice (day of maximum sunlight intensity) and the hottest day of the year. Use the values for $I_0$ and $I_1$ given for College Park in Figure 2, and assume a mean temperature of 283 K. Show work indicating the method of your calculations for the numbers plotted on the graph.

parts.label: f.
parts.statement:
Actual temperature data for College Park is shown in Figure 3. Does the model provide a reasonable fit to the data? Briefly justify your answer. (The summer solstice occurs on June 21.)

[[figure:p6-fig3]]

Figure 3: Actual average temperature data at Baltimore-Washington International Airport. The vertical line is June 30. Source: Weather Underground, [http://www.wunderground.com/](http://www.wunderground.com/).
